title: HOST: Robots Acquire Manipulation Skills in Seconds from a Single Human Video
paper_type_rationale: HOST is a novel AI method for robot skill acquisition from a single human video via cascade self-grounded prediction. Three-stage architecture (Localization → Vision → Action) plus retrieval-based skill retention. Strong empirical results on 7 real-robot tasks.

central_claims.claim: Cascade self-grounded prediction (Localization → Vision → Action) enables one-shot skill acquisition from a single human video, without any robot demonstrations or fine-tuning.
supporting_evidence: Fig 3B: Novel task success 62% vs AWDA 19% (+43pp)
T_i skill acquisition time: 29s average per task
central_claims.what_it_actually_proves: The three-stage self-grounded cascade is sufficient to learn manipulation skills from a single human video, bypassing the video-video matching bottleneck that plagues prior cross-embodiment work.
central_claims.what_it_does_not_prove: Whether the method scales beyond tabletop manipulation (no mobile/humanoid validation); whether progress manifold capacity limits how many distinct skills can be stored.

central_claims.claim: Coupling prediction targets to the demonstration via a shared progress manifold bypasses cross-embodiment video-video matching.
supporting_evidence: Fig 1B: HOST avoids Embodiment/Object/Scene/Viewpoint mismatch via progress coupling
Pipeline shows training objective (SDTW + TCC) and inference (Localization→Vision→Action) are aligned
central_claims.what_it_actually_proves: Progress is a cross-embodiment invariant, and projecting human video + robot trajectory onto a shared progress manifold eliminates the need for explicit video-video correspondence.
central_claims.what_it_does_not_prove: Whether the progress manifold generalizes to multi-modal tasks (e.g., language-conditioned) or scales to thousands of distinct skills.

central_claims.claim: Retrieval-based skill retention module preserves previously mastered skills (99% retention after 50 demos) by reusing past trajectory memory.
supporting_evidence: Fig 7: HOST 99% vs π0.5+SFT 20% vs Wall-OSS+SFT 43% (50 demos)
Fig 10E: Retrieval accuracy 100%/100% on mastered tasks at δ*=0.68
central_claims.what_it_actually_proves: Storing past demonstrations in a retrieval index and reusing them at inference time is a sufficient anti-forgetting mechanism for continual skill acquisition.
central_claims.what_it_does_not_prove: Whether the retrieval index scales to thousands of skills (no upper-bound evaluation); whether retrieval-based methods can match EWC/replay-buffer accuracy in domain-shifted settings.

central_claims.claim: 29-second average skill acquisition time + 62% novel-task success rate + 507× speed-up over SFT-50 baseline demonstrates practical value.
supporting_evidence: Fig 3B Time efficiency: HOST 29s vs SFT-10/20/50 at 2.5/3.0/4.0 hours
Fig 3B Data efficiency: 1 video = 62% vs 50 demos = 56%
Success rate: 62% novel task avg with single video
central_claims.what_it_actually_proves: The 1-video + 29-second acquisition workflow is genuinely competitive with full SFT pipelines, supporting the practical value of one-shot from-human-video skill acquisition.
central_claims.what_it_does_not_prove: Whether 62% is sufficient for production deployment (depends on task criticality); whether the speed-up holds when scaling to thousands of new skills over time.

claim_boundaries: 62% absolute success — still well below 1.0; method is a 'first 30 seconds' tool, not full autonomy.
Progress manifold quality caps the upper bound; visual-prediction errors compound at long horizons.
Human perturbation drops performance 9%; not yet robust to dynamic environmental changes.
Evaluated only on tabletop manipulation; not validated on mobile / humanoid / long-horizon loco-manipulation.
negative_or_limiting_results: Human perturbation -9% — single biggest robustness drop
Insert pen task lowest at 50% — fine-grained alignment is hard
Stage-1 pretraining is required: 0% without pretraining, scaling log-linear to 62%
comparative_positioning: HOST sits between one-shot imitation (no fine-tuning but lower success) and full SFT (high success but slow + catastrophic forgetting). The breakthrough is the **cascade self-grounded** mechanism that decouples skill acquisition from robot embodiment, paired with retrieval-based retention that solves the catastrophic forgetting problem of continual learning. Compared to WALL-SS (same team's earlier work on world models), HOST targets the lower-level skill acquisition loop rather than the world-model loop.
reuse_takeaways: Cascade self-grounded prediction is a credible alternative to cross-embodiment video-video matching.
Coupling via shared progress manifold is reusable whenever two trajectories share semantic task structure but differ in embodiment.
Retrieval-based retention is the lighter alternative to EWC / replay buffers for continual learning on robots.
29-second acquisition suggests near-real-time teleop+correction workflows are feasible.
followup_questions: Can cascade self-grounded combine with WALL-SS-style world models for closed-loop deployment?
What is the upper bound on progress manifold capacity — how many distinct skills can one model store?
How transferable is Stage-1 pretraining across robot embodiments (Franka / UR / ALOHA)?
Does HOST extend to mobile / humanoid / bimanual non-tabletop tasks?
